The Gospels consist primarily of story. Jesus goes places, does things. Most of this is not very quotable ("And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there"). The juicy bits are the bits which are (supposedly) actual quotes from Jesus. But even these are largely parables, and you can't just quote a single line out of a parable. So the actual quotable bits of the Gospels, where Jesus actually sits down and gives clear-cut instructions on what you should and should not do, come down to a rather slim slice of the whole four books -- and largely redundant, too.

The Letters, on the other hand (written by the Apostles to various faraway subbranches of the Chuch after the death of Jesus) consist pretty much entirely of clear-cut instructions on what you should and should not do -- exactly the kind of thing that you'd quote if you believed that it was actually true. It's full of juicy quotable stuff -- albeit from some guy Jesus knew rather than from Jesus himself, but most doctrines of Christianity hold that this stuff is just as important as the stuff that Jesus himself is quoted as having said.

As for the importance of the letter to the Romans -- I'm not sure, but wikipedia tells me it's the longest, so that probably has something to do with it.

Paul's letter to the Romans has always been considered the best insight as to how you should live your life as a Christian. Coming from Paul, this is especially important, considering who he was before his conversion.

While the gospels focus on history, the letters focus on theology. So if you believe the Bible, the letters do a good job of explaining what the events in the gospels mean. Also, the book of Romans gives a summarized explanation of what Christianity and the Gospel are. This means that Christians often quote Romans when trying to convince other people of their beliefs. Also, a devout Christian would generally believe that everything in the Bible is divinely inspired and thus true, so to them, both Romans and the gospels are reliable sources of information.
